newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden to seek Bofors papers from Switzerland.
newsitem.headline: Sweden to seek Bofors papers from Switzerland.

text.p: The Swedish government said on Tuesday it intended to appeal to Swiss courts to try to obtain a copy of secret bank documents relating to a billion dollar arms scandal that were handed over to India on Tuesday.

After seven years of legal wrangling, Switzerland released documents about Swiss bank accounts that were allegedly linked to a $1.3 billion artillery contract between Swedish arms manufacturer Bofors AB and the Indian government in 1986.

"The Swedish government is certainly interested, but since it did not participate in the deal there might be some legal difficulties in obtaining the information," Swedish government spokesman Leif-Ake Falk told Reuters.
India has been trying to investigate whether some leading politicians of the country were taking bribes over the arms deal with Bofors.
Swiss police said earlier it had evidence that Bofors paid $40 million to various accounts in Swiss banks.
The company has defended the deposits, saying these were payments for its agents.
Falk said the first step for Sweden was to obtain a copy of the court's verdict that agreed to release the documents.
"I assume that Sweden's government will take the initiative in the near future to acquire the verdict," Falk said.
"But it is too early to speculate how far the Swedish government will go in investigating the matters which took place 10 years ago."

In Bern on Tuesday, India's ambassador to Switzerland, Kizhakke Pisharath Balakrishnan, and head of India's Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), Joginder Singh, received a sealed box with some 500 pages of documents.
Singh said the papers allowed India to begin digging into the case.
The furore over the alleged bribes contributed to the defeat in 1989 of the government led by late prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, who was accused of involvement in the affair.
A Swedish commission investigating the 1986 murder of Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme was also reported by Swedish media to be interested in getting copies of the documents.
Palme, who was shot dead by an unknown assassin in a Stockholm street, worked closely with Gandhi to arrange the Bofors contract. It was finalised a month after his death.
